claim: CyTOF-Lec is an approach to simultaneously characterize many protein and glycan features of human immune cells at the single-cell level.
source: Here, we develop CyTOF-Lec as an approach to simultaneously characterize many protein and glycan features of human immune cells at the single-cell level.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the development of CyTOF-Lec and its capability to characterize both protein and glycan features at single-cell level.

claim: HIV upregulates the levels of cell-surface fucose in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Using bioinformatics approaches to distinguish preferential infection of cellular subsets from viral-induced remodeling, we demonstrate that HIV upregulates the levels of cell-surface fucose and sialic acid in a cell-intrinsic manner, and that memory CD4+ T cells co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid are highly susceptible to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract states this finding was demonstrated using bioinformatics approaches (PP-SLIDE) to distinguish viral-induced remodeling from preferential infection.

claim: HIV upregulates the levels of cell-surface sialic acid in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Using bioinformatics approaches to distinguish preferential infection of cellular subsets from viral-induced remodeling, we demonstrate that HIV upregulates the levels of cell-surface fucose and sialic acid in a cell-intrinsic manner, and that memory CD4+ T cells co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid are highly susceptible to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract states this finding was demonstrated using bioinformatics approaches to distinguish viral-induced remodeling from preferential infection.

claim: Memory CD4+ T cells co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid are highly susceptible to HIV infection.
source: Using bioinformatics approaches to distinguish preferential infection of cellular subsets from viral-induced remodeling, we demonstrate that HIV upregulates the levels of cell-surface fucose and sialic acid in a cell-intrinsic manner, and that memory CD4+ T cells co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid are highly susceptible to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on bioinformatics approaches.

claim: Sialic acid levels distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors.
source: Sialic acid levels were found to distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors, pro-survival factors, homing receptors, and activation markers, and to play a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sialic acid levels distinguish subsets with different expression of viral entry receptors.

claim: Sialic acid levels distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of pro-survival factors.
source: Sialic acid levels were found to distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors, pro-survival factors, homing receptors, and activation markers, and to play a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sialic acid levels distinguish subsets with different expression of pro-survival factors.

claim: Sialic acid levels distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of homing receptors.
source: Sialic acid levels were found to distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors, pro-survival factors, homing receptors, and activation markers, and to play a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sialic acid levels distinguish subsets with different expression of homing receptors.

claim: Sialic acid levels distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of activation markers.
source: Sialic acid levels were found to distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors, pro-survival factors, homing receptors, and activation markers, and to play a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sialic acid levels distinguish subsets with different expression of activation markers.

claim: Sialic acid plays a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
source: Sialic acid levels were found to distinguish memory CD4+ T cell subsets expressing different amounts of viral entry receptors, pro-survival factors, homing receptors, and activation markers, and to play a direct role in memory CD4+ T cells' susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sialic acid plays a direct role in susceptibility to HIV infection.

claim: The ability of sialic acid to distinguish memory CD4+ T cells with different susceptibilities to HIV infection was experimentally validated through sorting experiments.
source: The ability of sialic acid to distinguish memory CD4+ T cells with different susceptibilities to HIV infection was experimentally validated through sorting experiments.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that sorting experiments validated the ability of sialic acid to distinguish cells with different HIV susceptibilities.

claim: HIV remodels cellular glycans in addition to cellular proteins.
source: Together, these results suggest that HIV remodels not only cellular proteins but also glycans, and that glycan expression can differentiate memory CD4+ T cells with vastly different susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that HIV remodels both proteins and glycans.

claim: Glycan expression can differentiate memory CD4+ T cells with vastly different susceptibility to HIV infection.
source: Together, these results suggest that HIV remodels not only cellular proteins but also glycans, and that glycan expression can differentiate memory CD4+ T cells with vastly different susceptibility to HIV infection.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that glycan expression can differentiate memory CD4+ T cells with different HIV susceptibility.

claim: Viruses generally need to hijack multiple host cell processes to complete their replication cycle.
source: Viruses generally need to hijack multiple host cell processes to complete their replication cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Viral-induced remodeling of primary cells was studied at the single-cell level by characterizing, via cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF), human tonsillar T cells infected ex vivo by varicella zoster virus (VZV) (Sen et al., 2014).
source: More recently, viral remodeling of primary cells was studied at the single-cell level by characterizing, via cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF), human tonsillar T cells infected ex vivo by varicella zoster virus (VZV) (Sen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Sen et al., 2014).

claim: VZV infection elicits significant host cell remodeling and alters the skin-trafficking property of subsets of infected cells.
source: Bioinformatics analyses of high-dimensional CyTOF datasets of VZV-infected cells revealed that VZV infection elicits significant host cell remodeling and alters the skin-trafficking property of subsets of infected cells.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Sen et al., 2014).

claim: PP-SLIDE was implemented to document HIV-induced remodeling of T cells from blood, lymph node, and genital tract.
source: We recently implemented a follow-up approach, termed predicted precursor as determined by single-cell linkage using distance estimation (PP-SLIDE), to document HIV-induced remodeling of T cells from blood, lymph node, and genital tract, define the subsets of cells most susceptible to HIV infection, and characterize the phenotypes of HIV-infected cells in viremic and virally suppressed PLWH (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors.

claim: PP-SLIDE enables assessment of whether a receptor differentially expressed on HIV-infected cells reflects HIV-induced remodeling or preferential infection of cells harboring that pattern of expression of the receptor.
source: One important feature of PP-SLIDE is that it enables assessment of whether a receptor differentially expressed on HIV-infected cells reflects HIV-induced remodeling or preferential infection of cells harboring that pattern of expression of the receptor.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the PP-SLIDE method.

claim: HIV downregulates CD4 and CD28 receptors rather than preferentially infecting CD4LowCD28Low T cells.
source: For example, PP-SLIDE established that HIV-infected T cells express low levels of CD4 and CD28 not because HIV preferentially infects CD4LowCD28Low T cells, but rather because HIV downregulates these receptors (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021), which were independently shown to be down-modulated by HIV accessory genes (Garcia and Miller, 1991; Swigut et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors and others.

claim: CD4 and CD28 are down-modulated by HIV accessory genes (Garcia and Miller, 1991; Swigut et al., 2001).
source: For example, PP-SLIDE established that HIV-infected T cells express low levels of CD4 and CD28 not because HIV preferentially infects CD4LowCD28Low T cells, but rather because HIV downregulates these receptors (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021), which were independently shown to be down-modulated by HIV accessory genes (Garcia and Miller, 1991; Swigut et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies (Garcia and Miller, 1991; Swigut et al., 2001).

claim: HIV remodels surface receptors involved in T cell migration to lymph nodes and markers of Tfh cells.
source: Other HIV-remodeled surface receptors identified by PP-SLIDE include those involved in T cell migration to lymph nodes and markers of Tfh cells (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors.

claim: The low levels of surface CD127 expression on HIV-infected tonsillar T cells reflected preferential sparing of CD127High T cells from productive infection.
source: By contrast, the low levels of surface CD127 expression on HIV-infected tonsillar T cells reflected preferential sparing of CD127High T cells from productive infection (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors.

claim: CD127High memory T cells preferentially undergo latent infection by HIV (Hsiao et al., 2020).
source: Subsequent studies demonstrated that CD127High memory T cells preferentially undergo latent infection by HIV (Hsiao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Hsiao et al., 2020).

claim: PP-SLIDE-generated findings of preferential infection of cellular subsets have been experimentally validated through a variety of sorting experiments (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021).
source: These and other PP-SLIDE-generated findings of preferential infection of cellular subsets have been experimentally validated through a variety of sorting experiments (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Neidleman et al., 2020b; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors.

claim: Important insights into HIV pathogenesis and persistence can be gained from characterizing HIV-induced remodeling of primary cells at a single-cell level.
source: Together, these studies suggest that important insights into HIV pathogenesis and persistence can be gained from characterizing HIV-induced remodeling of primary cells at a single-cell level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from previous studies cited.

claim: All phenotypic characterizations of virally infected cells to date have only examined the cells' proteomes.
source: However, such remodeling studies – and in fact all phenotypic characterizations of virally infected cells to date – have only examined the cells' proteomes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in regulating multiple cellular processes and immune functions (Barrera et al., 2002).
source: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in regulating multiple cellular processes and immune functions (Barrera et al., 2002), as well as cell-cell (de Freitas Junior et al., 2011) and cell-pathogen (Colomb et al., 2019; Everest-Dass et al., 2012; Giron et al., 2020b) interactions.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in cell-cell interactions (de Freitas Junior et al., 2011).
source: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in regulating multiple cellular processes and immune functions (Barrera et al., 2002), as well as cell-cell (de Freitas Junior et al., 2011) and cell-pathogen (Colomb et al., 2019; Everest-Dass et al., 2012; Giron et al., 2020b) interactions.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (de Freitas Junior et al., 2011).

claim: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in cell-pathogen interactions (Colomb et al., 2019; Everest-Dass et al., 2012; Giron et al., 2020b).
source: Cell-surface glycosylation plays critical roles in regulating multiple cellular processes and immune functions (Barrera et al., 2002), as well as cell-cell (de Freitas Junior et al., 2011) and cell-pathogen (Colomb et al., 2019; Everest-Dass et al., 2012; Giron et al., 2020b) interactions.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Multiple viruses (e.g., HSV-1, CMV, and HTLV1) have been shown to alter the surface glycosylation of infected cells (Hiraiwa et al., 2003; Kambara et al., 2002; Nyström et al., 2007; Nyström et al., 2009).
source: Furthermore, multiple viruses (e.g., HSV-1, CMV, and HTLV1) have been shown to alter the surface glycosylation of infected cells (Hiraiwa et al., 2003; Kambara et al., 2002; Nyström et al., 2007; Nyström et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Studies of host glycomes have been limited to analysis of bulk cells, using techniques such as mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography, and lectin microarrays (Chen et al., 2021).
source: To date, studies of host glycomes have been limited to analysis of bulk cells, using techniques such as mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography, and lectin microarrays (Chen et al., 2021), although bacteria have been characterized at the single-cell level using lectins (Leipold et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Bacteria have been characterized at the single-cell level using lectins (Leipold et al., 2011).
source: To date, studies of host glycomes have been limited to analysis of bulk cells, using techniques such as mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography, and lectin microarrays (Chen et al., 2021), although bacteria have been characterized at the single-cell level using lectins (Leipold et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Leipold et al., 2011).

claim: Bulk populations of CD4+ T cells with different glycan features harbor different levels of HIV transcripts (Colomb et al., 2020).
source: A recent study analyzing bulk populations of CD4+ T cells with different glycan features demonstrated that they harbor different levels of HIV transcripts (Colomb et al., 2020), suggesting that the host cell glycome can affect HIV susceptibility and/or replication.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Colomb et al., 2020).

claim: The host cell glycome can affect HIV susceptibility and/or replication.
source: A recent study analyzing bulk populations of CD4+ T cells with different glycan features demonstrated that they harbor different levels of HIV transcripts (Colomb et al., 2020), suggesting that the host cell glycome can affect HIV susceptibility and/or replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited study (Colomb et al., 2020).

claim: Robust tools to deeply characterize, at the single-cell level, the glycan features of immune cells – including HIV-infected ones – are lacking to date.
source: However, robust tools to deeply characterize, at the single-cell level, the glycan features of immune cells – including HIV-infected ones – are lacking to date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the field.

claim: Lanthanide-conjugated lectins have previously been validated at the bulk level (Leipold et al., 2009).
source: This was achieved through conjugating a collection of lectins (proteins that specifically bind different types of glycans) to metal lanthanides, an approach that has previously been validated at the bulk level (Leipold et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Leipold et al., 2009).

claim: Antibody staining for CD3, CD4, and CD8 was the same whether or not the specimens were subsequently stained with lectins.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that antibody binding to CD3, CD4, and CD8 was the same whether or not the specimens were subsequently stained with lectins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A showing overlapping histograms.

claim: Binding by WGA and MAL-1 was decreased after sialidase treatment of the cells.
source: As expected, binding by WGA and MAL-1, which detect different forms of sialic acid (Supplementary file 1), was decreased after sialidase treatment of the cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing decreased binding after sialidase treatment.

claim: Binding by AOL and UEA-1 was increased after sialidase treatment of the cells.
source: By contrast, binding by AOL and UEA-1, which detect different forms of fucose, and ABA, which detects T antigen (Supplementary file 1), were all increased (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C-D showing increased binding after sialidase treatment.

claim: Binding by ABA was increased after sialidase treatment of the cells.
source: By contrast, binding by AOL and UEA-1, which detect different forms of fucose, and ABA, which detects T antigen (Supplementary file 1), were all increased (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C-D showing increased binding after sialidase treatment.

claim: Removal of sialic acid enables better detection of fucose and T antigen glycan structures.
source: This was expected as removal of sialic acid should enable better detection of these other glycan structures, and is consistent with prior reports (Giron et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is consistent with prior reports (Giron et al., 2020b) and expected based on glycan structure.

claim: AOL bound more to CD4+ Tm and CD8+ Tm cells than to their respective naïve counterparts in all three sites (endometrium, tonsils, PBMCs).
source: For all three sites, the fucose-specific lectins AOL and UEA1 bound more to CD4+ Tm and CD8+ Tm cells than to their respective naïve counterparts, although the difference only reached significance for AOL binding in tonsils (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with box plots comparing binding levels.

claim: Core surface fucosylation is important for T cell activation, which is more prominent within the memory compartment (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).
source: These results are consistent with the known role of core surface fucosylation for T cell activation, which is more prominent within the memory compartment (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).

claim: WGA and MAL1 bound to memory T cells more than to their naïve counterparts.
source: The sialic acid-binding lectins WGA and MAL1 also consistently bound to memory T cells more than to their naïve counterparts, although this only reached statistical significance for MAL1 binding of endometrial CD8+ T cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with box plots comparing binding levels.

claim: Binding by all five lectins was low on B cells, particularly as compared to memory CD8+ T cells.
source: Binding by all five lectins was low on B cells, particularly as compared to memory CD8+ T cells (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C with box plots comparing binding levels.

claim: Endometrial T cells were the most susceptible to HIV-F4.HSA infection.
source: Consistent with our prior studies (Ma et al., 2020), endometrial T cells were the most susceptible to HIV-F4.HSA infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and is consistent with prior studies (Ma et al., 2020).

claim: HIV-infected cells from all three sites (endometrium, tonsils, PBMCs) were remodeled.
source: HIV-infected cells from all three sites were remodeled, as established qualitatively by assessing their locations on a t-SNE (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) as well as quantitatively using SLIDE (Sen et al., 2014; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and 2C using t-SNE and SLIDE analysis.

claim: The PRE cells from all three sites were preferentially memory CD4+ T cells.
source: As expected (Ma et al., 2020), the PRE cells from all three sites were preferentially memory CD4+ T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and 3C and is consistent with prior studies (Ma et al., 2020).

claim: Both fucose and sialic acid were upregulated during HIV infection.
source: Interestingly, we found that both fucose and sialic acid were upregulated during HIV infection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of infected vs. PRE cells.

claim: Infected cells from all three sites potently upregulated total fucose as assessed by AOL binding.
source: Infected cells from all three sites potently upregulated total fucose as assessed by AOL binding (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), although this upregulation did not reach statistical significance (after correcting for multiple comparisons) for the endometrium.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A with box plots and histograms.

claim: Binding by UEA1 was not significantly different between infected and PRE cells.
source: Binding by UEA1, however, was not significantly different between infected and PRE cells, and tended to be downregulated in the endometrium and tonsils, and upregulated in PBMCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with box plots.

claim: Fucosylation is globally upregulated upon infection of tissue CD4+ T cells with HIV, although not the type of fucosylation that creates α1–2 branched structure.
source: As UEA1 binds α1–2 branched fucose (Supplementary file 1), these results suggest that fucosylation is globally upregulated upon infection of tissue CD4+ T cells with HIV, although not the type of fucosylation that creates α1–2 branched structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential binding patterns of AOL and UEA1.

claim: Both sialic acid-binding lectins (WGA and MAL-1) were increased on infected compared to PRE cells.
source: In contrast to the fucose-binding lectins, both sialic acid-binding lectins were increased on infected compared to PRE cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), and this was observed for all three sites although results did not reach statistical significance for the endometrium.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B with box plots and histograms.

claim: HIV upregulates both total sialic acid (recognized by WGA) and α2–3 linked sialic acid (recognized by MAL-1) during infection.
source: These results are consistent with an upregulation of both total sialic acid (recognized by WGA, which also binds to N-acetylglucosamine [GlcNAc]) (Schwarz et al., 1999) and α2–3 linked sialic acid (recognized by MAL-1) by HIV during infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased binding of WGA and MAL-1 on infected cells.

claim: No marked upregulation of T antigen was observed on infected cells.
source: In contrast to fucose and sialic acid, we did not observe any marked upregulation of T antigen on infected cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with box plots.

claim: In blood and tonsils, HIV preferentially infects memory CD4+ T cells with higher levels of fucose and sialic acid.
source: These results together with the remodeling analysis suggest that in blood and tonsils (but not endometrium), HIV preferentially infects memory CD4+ T cells with higher levels of fucose and sialic acid, and then further upregulates these cell-surface glycans through viral remodeling.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PRE cells to uninfected cells and infected cells.

claim: HIV further upregulates fucose and sialic acid on infected cells through viral remodeling.
source: These results together with the remodeling analysis suggest that in blood and tonsils (but not endometrium), HIV preferentially infects memory CD4+ T cells with higher levels of fucose and sialic acid, and then further upregulates these cell-surface glycans through viral remodeling.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PRE cells to infected cells.

claim: Increased binding by all five lectins was observed among bystander tonsillar CD4+ Tm cells relative to their counterparts from uninfected cultures.
source: Increased binding by all five lectins was observed among bystander tonsillar CD4+ Tm cells relative to their counterparts from uninfected cultures (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that in at least some tissue sites, remodeling of glycans on bystander CD4+ T cells occurs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 with box plots.

claim: Remodeling of glycans on bystander CD4+ T cells occurs in at least some tissue sites.
source: Increased binding by all five lectins was observed among bystander tonsillar CD4+ Tm cells relative to their counterparts from uninfected cultures (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), suggesting that in at least some tissue sites, remodeling of glycans on bystander CD4+ T cells occurs.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased lectin binding on bystander cells.

claim: Relative to bystander CD4+ Tm cells, the infected cells exhibited higher levels of total fucose and sialic acid.
source: Interestingly, however, relative to the bystander CD4+ Tm cells, the infected cells still exhibited higher levels of total fucose and sialic acid (as assessed by AOL and WGA binding, respectively), suggesting possible additional cell-intrinsic glycan remodeling by replicating virus (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 with box plots.

claim: Additional cell-intrinsic glycan remodeling by replicating virus is possible.
source: Interestingly, however, relative to the bystander CD4+ Tm cells, the infected cells still exhibited higher levels of total fucose and sialic acid (as assessed by AOL and WGA binding, respectively), suggesting possible additional cell-intrinsic glycan remodeling by replicating virus (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher glycan levels on infected vs. bystander cells.

claim: Only tonsils exhibited significant differences in glycan expression between uninfected vs. bystander cells among multiple subsets of B and T cells.
source: To examine whether HIV alters glycan expression in other bystander cellular subsets, we compared glycan levels on multiple subsets of B and T cells from the uninfected vs. infected cultures (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). Only tonsils exhibited significant differences between uninfected vs. bystander cells, and these differences were observed among all subsets.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6 with box plots.

claim: Sialic acid levels were significantly higher in all the analyzed subsets of bystander B, CD8+, and CD4+ T cells from tonsils, relative to their counterparts from uninfected cultures.
source: For example, sialic acid levels (as assessed by both WGA and MAL-1 binding) were significantly higher in all the analyzed subsets of bystander B, CD8+, and CD4+ T cells, relative to their counterparts from uninfected cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Fucose expression was uniformly higher among bystander cells from tonsils, although the difference among CD8+ Tm cells did not reach statistical significance.
source: Fucose expression was also uniformly higher among bystander cells, although the difference among CD8+ Tm cells did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Glycan changes in bystander cells may be elicited by HIV infection-induced inflammatory cytokines (Breen et al., 1990; Contreras et al., 2003; Sugawara et al., 2019).
source: These glycan changes may be elicited by HIV infection-induced inflammatory cytokines (Breen et al., 1990; Contreras et al., 2003; Sugawara et al., 2019), which can alter cell-surface glycosylation patterns (Dewald et al., 2016; Giron et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies on inflammatory cytokines and glycosylation.

claim: Inflammatory cytokines can alter cell-surface glycosylation patterns (Dewald et al., 2016; Giron et al., 2020a).
source: These glycan changes may be elicited by HIV infection-induced inflammatory cytokines (Breen et al., 1990; Contreras et al., 2003; Sugawara et al., 2019), which can alter cell-surface glycosylation patterns (Dewald et al., 2016; Giron et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies (Dewald et al., 2016; Giron et al., 2020a).

claim: AOLHigh and WGAHigh cells exhibited significantly higher HIV infection rates than did AOLLow and WGALow cells in both blood and both tissue compartments.
source: In both blood and both tissue compartments, AOLHigh and WGAHigh cells exhibited significantly higher HIV infection rates than did AOLLow and WGALow cells, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with box plots.

claim: The percentages of cells expressing high levels of AOL or WGA were higher among PRE cells in both tonsils and PBMCs.
source: Consistent with the MSI data, the percentages of cells expressing high levels of AOL or WGA were higher among PRE cells in both tonsils and PBMCs (Figure 4B), suggesting preferential infection of fucose- and sialic acid-expressing cells by HIV at these sites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with box plots.

claim: HIV preferentially infects fucose- and sialic acid-expressing cells in tonsils and PBMCs.
source: Consistent with the MSI data, the percentages of cells expressing high levels of AOL or WGA were higher among PRE cells in both tonsils and PBMCs (Figure 4B), suggesting preferential infection of fucose- and sialic acid-expressing cells by HIV at these sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher percentages of AOLHigh and WGAHigh cells among PRE cells.

claim: AOLHigh WGAHigh cells were significantly over-represented among PRE cells in tonsils and PBMCs.
source: Interestingly, AOLHigh WGAHigh cells were also significantly over-represented among PRE cells at these sites (Figure 4B), suggesting that the HIV-susceptible Tm cells co-express fucose and sialic acid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with box plots.

claim: The HIV-susceptible Tm cells co-express fucose and sialic acid.
source: Interestingly, AOLHigh WGAHigh cells were also significantly over-represented among PRE cells at these sites (Figure 4B), suggesting that the HIV-susceptible Tm cells co-express fucose and sialic acid.
evidence: This is inferred from the over-representation of AOLHigh WGAHigh cells among PRE cells.

claim: PRE cells co-expressing AOL and WGA could be detected from the endometrium.
source: Although PRE cells from the endometrium did not preferentially express fucose or sialic acid (Figure 4B), PRE cells co-expressing AOL and WGA could be detected from this site (Figure 4C), suggesting the endometrium, like the other two sites, harbors HIV-susceptible cells co-expressing fucose and sialic acid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with t-SNE plots.

claim: The endometrium harbors HIV-susceptible cells co-expressing fucose and sialic acid.
source: Although PRE cells from the endometrium did not preferentially express fucose or sialic acid (Figure 4B), PRE cells co-expressing AOL and WGA could be detected from this site (Figure 4C), suggesting the endometrium, like the other two sites, harbors HIV-susceptible cells co-expressing fucose and sialic acid.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of PRE cells co-expressing AOL and WGA.

claim: WGA is expressed at the highest levels on endometrial CD4+ Tm cells compared to tonsillar and blood CD4+ Tm cells.
source: To better understand why the HIV-susceptible endometrial CD4+ Tm cells, unlike their tonsillar and blood counterparts, did not preferentially express high levels sialic acid or fucose, we compared the levels of WGA and AOL binding on uninfected CD4+ Tm cells from the three sites. This analysis revealed WGA, but not AOL, to be expressed at the highest levels on the endometrial cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D with box plots.

claim: The reason WGAHigh cells are not preferentially targeted for infection in the endometrium may be that endometrial CD4+ Tm cells all express high levels of sialic acid.
source: These results suggest that the reason WGAHigh cells are not preferentially targeted for infection in the endometrium may be that endometrial CD4+ Tm cells all express high levels of sialic acid.
evidence: This is inferred from the high levels of WGA expression on endometrial CD4+ Tm cells.

claim: Among blood and tonsillar memory CD4+ T cells, those with the highest levels of fucose and sialic acid are preferentially targeted for infection by HIV.
source: All together, these results suggest that among blood and tonsillar memory CD4+ T cells, those with the highest levels of fucose and sialic acid are preferentially targeted for infection by HIV; this phenomenon was however not observed among endometrial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of PRE cells and infection rates.

claim: Enriched clusters identified by FlowSOM correspond to cells preferentially harboring HIV-susceptible cells.
source: Enriched clusters identified in this manner (corresponding to those preferentially harboring HIV-susceptible cells, see Materials and methods) were detected among all three sites, with eight clusters from the endometrium, nine from tonsils, and six from PBMCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with enrichment ratios.

claim: The fold-enrichment was highest among the tonsils, suggesting that of all three sites, this one exhibits the most preferential selection of subsets for infection.
source: Interestingly, the fold-enrichment was highest among the tonsils (reaching almost 20-fold in one donor), suggesting that of all three sites, this one exhibits the most preferential selection of subsets for infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with enrichment ratios.

claim: Compared to the other two sites, the tonsils harbored more enriched clusters with significantly elevated levels of fucose, sialic acid, and T antigens relative to their expression levels on uninfected CD4+ Tm cells.
source: Compared to the other two sites, the tonsils also harbored more enriched clusters with significantly elevated levels of fucose, sialic acid, and T antigens relative to their expression levels on uninfected CD4+ Tm cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with box plots.

claim: The enriched clusters from all three sites include cells expressing high levels of both fucose and sialic acid.
source: This analysis revealed regions of the t-SNEs co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid (Figure 5C), confirming the manual gating data that HIV-susceptible cells co-express these two classes of glycans.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with t-SNE heatmaps.

claim: HIV-susceptible cells co-express fucose and sialic acid.
source: This analysis revealed regions of the t-SNEs co-expressing high levels of fucose and sialic acid (Figure 5C), confirming the manual gating data that HIV-susceptible cells co-express these two classes of glycans.
evidence: This is confirmed by both manual gating and FlowSOM analysis.

claim: Infection rates directly correlated with the expression levels of sialic acid in sorted CD4+ Tm cells from blood.
source: Infection rates directly correlated with the expression levels of sialic acid, with the WGALow cells being the least susceptible and the WGAHigh the most (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and C with FACS plots and compiled results.

claim: In PBMCs, differentially susceptible CD4+ Tm cells can be isolated based solely on sialic acid expression levels.
source: These results provide experimental confirmation that in PBMCs, differentially susceptible CD4+ Tm cells can be isolated based solely on sialic acid expression levels.
evidence: This is confirmed by the sorting experiments showing differential infection rates.

claim: WGAHigh Tm cells bind more AOL than WGALow Tm cells do.
source: The WGAHigh cells preferentially expressed fucose (as assessed by AOL binding) (Figure 6D), consistent with earlier observations of co-expression of fucose and sialic acid on HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D with histograms and box plots.

claim: WGAHigh cells preferentially expressed higher levels of CD4 and the HIV co-receptor CCR5 relative to their WGALow counterparts.
source: Relative to their WGALow counterparts, the WGAHigh cells also preferentially expressed higher levels of CD4 and the HIV co-receptor CCR5 (Figure 6E), potentially explaining the increased susceptibility of these cells to infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E with histograms and box plots.

claim: Six markers of T cell activation (HLADR, CD69, CD38, CD25, CD28, and ICOS) were all elevated on WGAHigh cells compared to WGALow cells.
source: As activated T cells are known to be preferentially susceptible to infection (Stevenson et al., 1990), we also compared expression levels of activation markers on the WGALow and WGAHigh cells, and found that six markers of T cell activation (HLADR, CD69, CD38, CD25, CD28, and ICOS) were all elevated on the latter population (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F with histograms and box plots.

claim: Activated T cells are known to be preferentially susceptible to infection (Stevenson et al., 1990).
source: As activated T cells are known to be preferentially susceptible to infection (Stevenson et al., 1990), we also compared expression levels of activation markers on the WGALow and WGAHigh cells, and found that six markers of T cell activation (HLADR, CD69, CD38, CD25, CD28, and ICOS) were all elevated on the latter population (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Stevenson et al., 1990).

claim: Stimulated CD4+ Tm cells expressed higher levels of multiple activation markers compared to resting CD4+ Tm cells.
source: As expected, the stimulated CD4+ Tm cells expressed higher levels of multiple activation markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a with histograms.

claim: Stimulated CD4+ Tm cells bound higher levels of WGA compared to resting CD4+ Tm cells.
source: Importantly, the stimulated CD4+ Tm cells also bound higher levels of WGA, consistent with upregulation of sialic acid upon T cell activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with box plots.

claim: Activated cells, as defined as those expressing high levels HLADR, CD69, CD38, CD25, CD28, or ICOS, all expressed higher levels of sialic acid as compared to cells with low levels of these activation markers.
source: Furthermore, activated cells, as defined as those expressing high levels HLADR, CD69, CD38, CD25, CD28, or ICOS, all expressed higher levels of sialic acid as compared to cells with low levels of these activation markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with box plots.

claim: High sialic expression identifies the most activated subsets of CD4+ Tm cells.
source: These data together strongly support the notion that high sialic expression identifies the most activated subsets of CD4+ Tm cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between sialic acid expression and activation markers.

claim: WGAHigh cells expressed higher levels of CD127, a marker of long-lived self-renewing cells.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that WGAHigh cells expressed higher levels of CD127, a marker of long-lived self-renewing cells, and Ox40 and BIRC5, which are involved in protecting HIV-infected cells from apoptosis (Kuo et al., 2018; Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G with histograms and box plots.

claim: WGAHigh cells expressed higher levels of Ox40 and BIRC5, which are involved in protecting HIV-infected cells from apoptosis (Kuo et al., 2018).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that WGAHigh cells expressed higher levels of CD127, a marker of long-lived self-renewing cells, and Ox40 and BIRC5, which are involved in protecting HIV-infected cells from apoptosis (Kuo et al., 2018; Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G with histograms and box plots, and cited from a previous study (Kuo et al., 2018).

claim: Markers preferentially expressed on the WGALow cells were those of central memory T cells, including CD27, CCR7, and CD62L.
source: In comparison, markers preferentially expressed on the WGALow cells were those of central memory T cells, including CD27, CCR7, and CD62L (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H with histograms and box plots.

claim: Sialidase treatment decreased cell-surface sialic acid levels on CD4+ T cells.
source: Inhibitor treatment did not decrease cell-surface sialic acid levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but sialidase did (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I with overlaid histograms.

claim: Infection rates were decreased in a sialidase dose-dependent manner.
source: We therefore exposed mock- or sialidase-treated cells to HIV-F4.HSA for 3 days and then assessed infection rates by FACS. We found that infection rates were decreased in a sialidase dose-dependent manner (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6J and K with FACS plots and compiled results.

claim: Sialic acid may play a direct role in promoting infection by HIV.
source: These results suggest that a single glycan – sialic acid – may not only be capable of distinguishing memory CD4+ T cells with vastly different phenotypic features and HIV susceptibility but may also play a direct role in promoting infection by the virus.
evidence: This is inferred from the sialidase treatment experiments showing decreased infection rates.

claim: HIV infection of cell lines leads to up- and downregulation of a variety of host proteins (Matheson et al., 2015).
source: Multiple studies have demonstrated remodeling of host cells upon HIV infection. HIV infection of cell lines (Matheson et al., 2015) as well as primary cells (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021) leads to up- and downregulation of a variety of host proteins, reflecting the ability of the virus to hijack host processes to complete its replication cycle.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Matheson et al., 2015).

claim: HIV infection of primary cells leads to up- and downregulation of a variety of host proteins (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021).
source: Multiple studies have demonstrated remodeling of host cells upon HIV infection. HIV infection of cell lines (Matheson et al., 2015) as well as primary cells (Cavrois et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021) leads to up- and downregulation of a variety of host proteins, reflecting the ability of the virus to hijack host processes to complete its replication cycle.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors.

claim: HIV also remodels the surface glycome of infected cells.
source: We demonstrate in the current study that HIV also remodels the surface glycome of infected cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study.

claim: Core fucosylation on the cell surface is critical for CD4+ T cell activation (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).
source: As core fucosylation on the cell surface is critical for CD4+ T cell activation (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018) and activated cells are more permissive to HIV infection (Stevenson et al., 1990), HIV may upregulate fucosylation to maintain an elevated state of activation facilitating the completion of its replication.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).

claim: HIV may upregulate fucosylation to maintain an elevated state of activation facilitating the completion of its replication.
source: As core fucosylation on the cell surface is critical for CD4+ T cell activation (Fujii et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018) and activated cells are more permissive to HIV infection (Stevenson et al., 1990), HIV may upregulate fucosylation to maintain an elevated state of activation facilitating the completion of its replication.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known roles of fucosylation and activation in HIV infection.

claim: Fucosylation is important for lymphocyte trafficking (Colomb et al., 2020).
source: Of note, fucosylation is also important for lymphocyte trafficking (Colomb et al., 2020), and the upregulation of fucose on infected cells, even if not directly promoting viral replication, may facilitate the circulation of infected cells from blood into tissues where ample populations of HIV-permissive CD4+ T cells reside.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Colomb et al., 2020).

claim: The upregulation of fucose on infected cells may facilitate the circulation of infected cells from blood into tissues where ample populations of HIV-permissive CD4+ T cells reside.
source: Of note, fucosylation is also important for lymphocyte trafficking (Colomb et al., 2020), and the upregulation of fucose on infected cells, even if not directly promoting viral replication, may facilitate the circulation of infected cells from blood into tissues where ample populations of HIV-permissive CD4+ T cells reside.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of fucosylation in lymphocyte trafficking.

claim: Binding of sialic acid on the surface of cancer cells to Siglec-7 and Siglec-9 proteins on the surface of NK cells can diminish NKG2D-mediated activation of the NK cells (Xiao et al., 2016).
source: In general, sialylated glycans on the surface of cells can elicit an immunosuppressive response by effector cells of the immune system. For example, binding of sialic acid on the surface of cancer cells to Siglec-7 and Siglec-9 proteins on the surface of NK cells can diminish NKG2D-mediated activation of the NK cells (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: NKG2D may play an important role in NK cell-mediated killing of HIV-infected cells and NKG2D ligands are actively downregulated by HIV Nef to escape immune recognition (Jost and Altfeld, 2012).
source: Moreover, NKG2D may play an important role in NK cell-mediated killing of HIV-infected cells and NKG2D ligands are actively downregulated by HIV Nef to escape immune recognition (Jost and Altfeld, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Jost and Altfeld, 2012).

claim: Through a combination of upregulating sialic acid and downregulating NKG2D ligands, HIV may evade NKG2D-mediated killing by NK cells.
source: We postulate that through a combination of upregulating sialic acid and downregulating NKG2D ligands, HIV may evade NKG2D-mediated killing by NK cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known roles of sialic acid and NKG2D ligands in immune evasion.

claim: The high levels of sialic acid on HIV-infected cells results from preferential infection of cellular subsets with high levels of cell-surface sialic acid, followed by further upregulation of this glycan.
source: Interestingly, sialic acid was also preferentially expressed on the memory CD4+ T cells that were preferentially targeted for infection by HIV. These results suggest that the high levels of sialic acid on HIV-infected cells results from preferential infection of cellular subsets with high levels of cell-surface sialic acid, followed by further upregulation of this glycan.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of PRE cells and infected cells.

claim: The preferential selection of WGAHigh memory CD4+ T cells for HIV infection was only observed in tonsils and PBMCs, but not in the endometrium.
source: Interestingly, however, the preferential selection of WGAHigh memory CD4+ T cells for HIV infection was only observed in tonsils and PBMCs, but not in the endometrium (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with box plots.

claim: Memory CD4+ T cells from the endometrium express higher levels of cell-surface sialic acid than those from tonsils or PBMCs.
source: Because memory CD4+ T cells from the endometrium express higher levels of cell-surface sialic acid than those from tonsils or PBMCs (Figure 4E), most endometrial memory CD4+ T cells may already have the WGAHigh HIV-permissive phenotype, resulting in minimal selection of these cells by HIV.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with box plots.

claim: Most endometrial memory CD4+ T cells may already have the WGAHigh HIV-permissive phenotype, resulting in minimal selection of these cells by HIV.
source: Because memory CD4+ T cells from the endometrium express higher levels of cell-surface sialic acid than those from tonsils or PBMCs (Figure 4E), most endometrial memory CD4+ T cells may already have the WGAHigh HIV-permissive phenotype, resulting in minimal selection of these cells by HIV.
evidence: This is inferred from the high levels of sialic acid on endometrial memory CD4+ T cells.

claim: Many subsets of endometrial memory CD4+ T cells are susceptible to HIV infection, as compared to a markedly lower number of HIV-susceptible memory CD4+ T cell subsets from the blood compartment (Ma et al., 2020).
source: Indeed, this would be consistent with the many subsets of endometrial memory CD4+ T cells that are susceptible to HIV infection, as compared to a markedly lower number of HIV-susceptible memory CD4+ T cell subsets from the blood compartment (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Ma et al., 2020).

claim: The endometrium serves as the site of blastocyst implantation and development of a semi-allogenic fetus.
source: It is also worthwhile to note that the endometrium is a unique tissue in that it serves as the site of blastocyst implantation and development of a semi-allogenic fetus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the endometrium.

claim: The unusually high levels of sialic acid on immune cells from the endometrium may be important to prevent immune-mediated rejection of spermatozoa or the developing fetus.
source: The unusually high levels of sialic acid on immune cells from this tissue may be important to prevent immune-mediated rejection of spermatozoa or the developing fetus.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known immunosuppressive role of sialic acid.

claim: WGA may be useful as a tool to isolate a highly susceptible population of CD4+ T cells.
source: Regardless, since thus far markers that distinguish memory CD4+ T cells with differing susceptibilities to HIV have been difficult to identify, our findings that WGA may be useful as a tool to isolate a highly susceptible population of CD4+ T cells could be of practical use for the field.
evidence: This is stated as a practical implication of the findings.

claim: Host glycan expression can influence HIV replication dynamics.
source: On a more fundamental level, our results suggest that host glycan expression can very much influence HIV replication dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: HIV particles contain cell-derived glycolipids, including the sialic acid-containing GM3 ganglioside (Puryear et al., 2012).
source: Of note, we cannot rule out the possibility that the high levels of fucose and sialic acid on HIV-infected cells may also result in part from binding of HIV virions to the surface of the infected CD4+ T cells. HIV particles contain cell-derived glycolipids, including the sialic acid-containing GM3 ganglioside (Puryear et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Puryear et al., 2012).

claim: HIV gp120 is heavily N-glycosylated, with a majority of high-mannose N-glycan structures and a lower proportion of complex N-glycans carrying lactosamine residues and terminal sialic acid.
source: Furthermore, HIV gp120 is heavily N-glycosylated, with a majority of high-mannose N-glycan structures and a lower proportion of complex N-glycans carrying lactosamine residues and terminal sialic acid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HIV gp120 glycosylation.

claim: Sialic acid on gp120 is recognized by multiple members of the Siglec family of lectins, and these lectins can facilitate trans- or cell-to-cell infection of CD4+ T cells (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012; Varchetta et al., 2013; Zou et al., 2011).
source: Sialic acid on gp120 is recognized by multiple members of the Siglec family of lectins, and these lectins can facilitate trans- or cell-to-cell infection of CD4+ T cells (Izquierdo-Useros et al., 2012; Varchetta et al., 2013; Zou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Productively infected cells have distinct cell-surface glycan features in a manner not attributable to just surface virion sticking.
source: However, we note that our studies characterizing infected cells defined these cells as those that express HSA – which is not on the surface of input virions – and that have downregulated cell-surface CD4, a hallmark of productive HIV infection. The fact that we found unique glycan features of these cells relative to bystander CD4+ T cells suggests that productively infected cells have distinct cell-surface glycan features in a manner not attributable to just surface virion sticking.
evidence: This is inferred from the unique glycan features of productively infected cells.

claim: WGA also binds GlcNAc, so some of the WGA effects observed may be due to GlcNAc and not sialic acid.
source: Second, while WGA is commonly used as a reagent to monitor cell-surface sialic acid levels, it also binds GlcNAc, so we cannot rule out that some of the WGA effects we observed were due to GlcNAc and not sialic acid.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Cell-surface GlcNAc is important for HIV binding and infection (Spillings et al., 2022).
source: Notably, a recent study reported that cell-surface GlcNAc is important for HIV binding and infection (Spillings et al., 2022), which is in line with our observation that WGAHigh cells are highly susceptible to HIV infection.
evidence: This is cited from a recent study (Spillings et al., 2022).

source: Recent observations suggest that a significant portion of the reservoir in ART-suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH) is transcriptionally active, expressing short and incomplete HIV transcripts in the absence of ex vivo stimulation (Yukl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Yukl et al., 2018).

source: Interestingly, we recently demonstrated using cells from ART-suppressed PLWH that CD4+ T cells expressing high levels of fucose contain significantly more transcriptionally active HIV reservoir cells than those expressing low levels of fucose (Colomb et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study by the authors (Colomb et al., 2020).

source: For example, influenza virus enters cells by binding of its hemagglutinin (HA) protein to terminal sialic acid moieties attached to surface proteins of host cells (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Li et al., 2021).

source: The novel beta-coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 may also exploit host cell glycosylation for infection, as its primary receptor ACE2 is heavily glycosylated.

claim: Blockage of N- and O-glycan synthesis on the host cell can inhibit SARS-CoV-2 entry by diminishing the ability of the viral spike protein to bind ACE2 (Yang et al., 2020).
source: Indeed, blockage of N- and O-glycan synthesis on the host cell can inhibit SARS-CoV-2 entry by diminishing the ability of the viral spike protein to bind ACE2 (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study (Yang et al., 2020).

claim: Better understanding the surface glycans of virally susceptible host cells through single-cell glycomic analysis by CyTOF-Lec can potentially lead to novel prophylactic or therapeutic agents for clinically relevant viral pathogens.
source: Better understanding the surface glycans of virally susceptible host cells through single-cell glycomic analysis by CyTOF-Lec, in conjunction with identifying the protein backbones harboring the glycans, will improve our understanding of viral pathogenesis and can potentially lead to novel prophylactic or therapeutic agents for clinically relevant viral pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of CyTOF-Lec.
